prompt: What problem is platform engineering actually solving? Isn't 'you build it, you run it' the goal?
answer_markdown: Full ownership was a real improvement over throwing code at an operations team, but taken literally it hands every product team the entire weight of modern infrastructure: container orchestration, infrastructure as code, pipeline design, secret management, network policy, dashboards, alert routing and a pager rotation. That is a specialism, and most product teams have neither the time nor the inclination to acquire it. The result is one of two expensive outcomes. Either teams move slowly, because standing up a new service takes weeks of infrastructure archaeology, or each team builds its own version — several pipeline shapes, several logging conventions, several ways of handling secrets, most of them subtly wrong. The second is worse than it looks, because it multiplies your operational surface by the number of teams and turns any organisation-wide fix, such as a base-image vulnerability, into many separate migrations. A platform absorbs that complexity once, so it is paid for by a team whose job it actually is.

prompt: How do you tell whether an internal platform is any good?
answer_markdown: The decisive test is whether teams choose it because it is genuinely easier, not because they are required to. A platform that has to be mandated is failing, and worse, the mandate conceals the evidence: high voluntary adoption proves value, while compulsory adoption tells you nothing about quality and creates a standing incentive for teams to route around you, which they will do in ways you typically discover during an incident. Beyond adoption, measure customer outcomes rather than platform output: time to first deploy for a brand-new service is the single most revealing number, alongside lead time for change and how much toil actually disappeared. Counting shipped platform features says nothing about whether anyone benefited. A useful sanity check is tickets per service — if ticket volume grows in proportion to the services hosted, the platform has centralised manual work rather than automating it.

prompt: Explain the difference between a golden path, a guardrail and a gate, and say which you should prefer.
answer_markdown: A golden path is a well-supported default route — the templated, documented, opinionated way to build a service, which is both easy and correct; it is a recommendation with the friction removed. A guardrail is an automated boundary that prevents disaster without blocking work, such as a network policy stopping a service reaching the internet, a quota capping spend, or an admission rule rejecting a container running as root: you are free to move, you just cannot drive off the cliff. A gate is a checkpoint that blocks until something or someone approves. You should prefer paths and guardrails, because gates impose a queue on every change and a queue is a bottleneck that grows with adoption — so the more successful your platform becomes, the slower everyone gets. Guardrails scale for free since they are enforced by machinery, apply uniformly and need nobody awake. Reserve gates for genuinely irreversible actions where being wrong costs more than waiting.

prompt: What is the leaky-abstraction risk in a platform, and how do you mitigate it?
answer_markdown: A platform necessarily hides complexity, and that is precisely its value — but an abstraction that hides Kubernetes until it breaks, then requires deep Kubernetes knowledge to debug, has made things strictly worse than no abstraction at all. The team never learned the underlying system because they never had reason to, so when the abstraction leaks they are debugging two unfamiliar systems simultaneously, under pressure, without even the vocabulary to search for help effectively. Three things mitigate it. Escape hatches let a team drop to the layer below for a legitimate case without abandoning the platform entirely. Errors phrased in the user's vocabulary — 'replicas must be at least 2 for tier critical' rather than a raw admission-webhook rejection — keep people unblocked without a ticket. And transparency about what was created lets a developer see which resources their manifest produced, so they gradually learn the mapping instead of being kept ignorant of it.

prompt: A team's requirements do not fit your golden path — they need a GPU node pool, an unsupported runtime and an unusual sidecar. What do you do?
answer_markdown: Refusing pushes them to build their own deployment path, leaving you with an unmanaged service plus a team telling everyone the platform is a straitjacket — you lose adoption and gain a shadow platform. Saying yes and building it bespoke takes on unfunded maintenance for a single customer, and repeating that leaves the platform team doing custom infrastructure work full-time with no capacity for the platform itself. The right answer is an escape hatch that keeps the platform's non-negotiables: the team writes their own deployment resources but still receives identity, secrets, network policy, logging and a catalogue entry, so they keep the guardrails and forgo only the golden path. The crucial extra step is logging the request, because the same escape hatch requested three times is a product signal that the golden path is missing something real, and the fourth requester should find it supported. That reasoning is what demonstrates you treat the platform as a product with a usage-informed roadmap rather than a fixed set of rules.

prompt: What is the classic failure mode of a platform team, and what does Team Topologies say a platform team is for?
answer_markdown: Team Topologies frames a platform team as an enabling structure whose purpose is reducing the cognitive load on stream-aligned product teams so they can genuinely own their services end to end. The classic failure mode is that the platform team becomes a ticket queue: every new service, permission or configuration change requires a request, so the platform team lands on everyone's critical path and the bottleneck it was created to remove has simply relocated. The tell is easy to spot — if the platform's primary interface is a request form rather than an API, a manifest or a repository, it is an operations team with a new name. The distinction matters because a self-service interface scales with the number of teams while a queue degrades with it, so the ticket-queue platform gets worse precisely as it succeeds in attracting users.

prompt: Why should a platform's manifest validator reject unknown fields rather than ignore them, and report all errors at once?
answer_markdown: Ignoring an unknown field turns a typo into a silent misconfiguration. If someone writes replicaz instead of replicas, a permissive validator discards it and provisions the default single replica while the developer genuinely believes they asked for three — a discrepancy that surfaces during an incident, which is the worst possible moment to learn your configuration never took effect. Rejecting unknown keys converts that into an immediate, obvious error at the only point where it is cheap to fix. Reporting all errors at once is about friction rather than correctness: returning only the first failure forces an edit-and-retry cycle per mistake, and the reputation of a platform as slow and annoying is built almost entirely from that kind of avoidable round-trip. Both decisions are examples of guardrails doing work that would otherwise require a gate or a support ticket, and both depend on error messages phrased in the developer's own vocabulary.
